query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: A Q235 steel sample whose native oxide layer is improved (made more continuous and chemically stable via controlled polishing and thermal annealing) will exhibit suppressed corrosion initiation and degradation under chloride‐rich conditions at both room and moderately elevated temperatures compared to untreated steel.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as‐received (pre-exposure) state with its native, heterogeneous oxide and defect distribution.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled surface treatment that systematically modifies the initial oxide layer on Q235 steel by a combination of gentle polishing to remove irregularities and subsequent thermal annealing in a controlled atmosphere to promote the formation of a continuous, defect‐reduced oxide film.
generation.conditions: Exposure to a chloride-rich corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) under controlled laboratory settings at room temperature (~25°C) and an elevated temperature (e.g., 70–90°C) while holding other environmental parameters constant (e.g., pH, humidity, and oxygen availability).
generation.structural_mediator: The quality and continuity of the native oxide film (with a more uniform composition and reduced defect sites) that acts as a barrier to corrosive attack.
generation.mechanism: By enhancing the continuity and stability of the oxide film, the treated steel minimizes active corrosion sites and suppresses localized anodic dissolution. This barrier effect limits the ingress of chloride ions and reduces the development of micro-cracks or pits that usually catalyze corrosion propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated Q235 steel, the pre-treated sample will show lower corrosion current densities (as measured via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy), reduced weight loss, and fewer or less-developed corrosion cracks/pitting after equivalent exposure durations in chloride-rich environments at both ambient and moderately elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel with its native, non-optimized oxide layer serving as the reference state.
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated under controlled laboratory corrosive conditions; however, extreme environmental conditions (e.g., very high chloride concentrations, very high temperatures, or additional mechanical stresses) could overwhelm the protective influence of the modified oxide layer.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how uniformly the controlled modification of the native oxide layer translates to long-term corrosion suppression in real-world complexities and whether additional microstructural factors (e.g., residual stress or inherent defect distribution) may also significantly influence the corrosion behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of Q235 steel samples: one set will undergo the controlled surface treatment (polishing followed by thermal annealing) to modify the native oxide, while the second set remains as-received. Both sets will be exposed to identical chloride-rich solutions (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) under two temperature conditions (room temperature ~25°C and elevated temperature ~70–90°C) for a fixed duration. Measurements will be made after set intervals.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to measure corrosion current densities and passive film characteristics.
Weight loss measurements to quantify total corrosion rates.
Microscopic (SEM) and surface analyses to assess crack formation, pitting, and oxide layer continuity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion current density, weight loss, and microstructural damage (e.g., crack/pit density) compared to the untreated samples under the specified conditions, then the hypothesis that the modified native oxide provides enhanced corrosion resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 7c shows the cross-section topography after high-temperature XRD oxidation in air. An irregular oxide scale formed and remained adherent to the substrate. The oxide scale thickness is about 1.58, 2.53, and 3.45 μm at different locations, which indicates that oxidation does not occur uniformly on the surface. Furthermore, no evidence of internal oxidation attack along the grain boundaries within the substrate was observed. In addition, no internal oxidation attack in the substrate is seen as having been executed along the grain boundaries. Figure 8 presents a cross-sectional EDS map of the specimen oxidized when heated during in situ XRD. For the specimen oxidized, it was observed that a mixed oxide layer consisting of Mn, Cr, and Fe oxides on the substrate and the oxides were confirmed to be Mn2O3, Mn3O4, Fe3Mn3O8, and MnCr2O4 when combined with XRD data shown in Figure 6. Mn- and Cr-depleted areas formed in the scale–substrate interface area, which are now filled with a high concentration of Ni, Co, and Fe. Kim et al. [] reported that a decrease in elements in the interface region may reduce the sluggish diffusion effect, which further influences high-temperature oxidation

It was noted that the shape and appearance of the cracks in the aerated testing were more curved and thinner in comparison with the cracks observed in the Al-HEA coating after the exposure in the wellhead test. The effect of a difference in temperature in the aerated and the wellhead, and hence the extent of thermal stresses, could explain to some extent this variance in cracking behavior. However, no corrosion products were observed in the cracks in the Al-HEA coating, and hence the cracking was concluded to have formed due to internal stresses in the coating.

To further investigate the interface of the corrosion reaction between solution and alloys, the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy test of the alloys in 0.5 M H2SO4 solution are shown in Figure 7. The Nyquist plot of the Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mo0.1 and 304 stainless steel alloys include one capacitive loop from high to low frequencies, revealing that the alloys are provided with a passivation layer when corroded. Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mo0.1 alloys only include one capacitive loop, resulting from the presence of Mo element in HEA. This element is present in the outer regions of the passive film as Mo(VI) and generates in its unoxidized state at the metallic matrix immediately beneath the film, which can be used as a barrier and inhibit the formation of adsorption layer []. On the other hand, a different behavior was observed in Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5 alloy. It includes two capacitive loops in electrochemical impedance diagrams, which are typically related to the presence of a passivation layer and an adsorption layer. decision.trend: Earlier studies in corrosion research on multi‐component alloys moved from general performance assessments in harsh environments toward isolating key chemical and microstructural contributions. For example, PMC6908586 dissected the role of elemental dissolution (Mn loss) and its secondary effects on protective Cr retention, while PMC8305802 demonstrated how controlled deposition processes and surface oxide formation can decisively influence corrosion resistance. However, while these studies have provided evidence that specific material states (such as oxide chemistry and elemental distributions) govern corrosion behavior at high temperatures and room temperature, they did not isolate and decisively falsify a single mechanistic cause relative to an untreated reference.
decision.unsolved: For Q235 steel in its as-received pre‐exposure state, the precise mechanistic origin that triggers or suppresses corrosion initiation remains ambiguous. There is a lack of controlled studies that modulate only one intrinsic factor (e.g., the state of the native oxide or defect density) while keeping environmental conditions constant, along with a predetermined falsification criterion that can decisively confirm or refute the hypothesized mechanism.
decision.lever: systematic modification of the initial oxide layer (via controlled polishing/thermal annealing) on Q235 steel combined with varying chloride concentration and temperature settings
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the trend of isolating single factors that govern corrosion. By precisely altering the native oxide and defect structure, one can test the hypothesis that the quality/composition of the pre‐exposure surface layer dictates anticorrosion behavior. The controlled variable experiment offers clear predictive outcomes (e.g., enhanced oxide quality should lead to lower corrosion rates under defined chloride-rich, ambient and elevated temperature conditions) and a decisive falsification criterion if the observed behavior deviates from these predictions.
